shouldFix.title: The supportingBytes entry that implements the unscoring still carries the v4-era note 'also authored', which is false in v5 and contradicts every operative statement of the repair
detail: The entry reads in full: { path: docs/coop/artifacts/fixtures/dr-103.v4/TC-PATH.unicode-norm-duplicate.manifest.json, sha256: afeb18c7..., note: 'also authored; listed so directory inventory includes v4-only bytes' }.

In v4 that note was true - the file was an authored TC-PATH member AND was listed in supportingBytes so the directory inventory covered v4-only bytes. v5's whole repair is that it is no longer authored: the authored entry is removed, authoredCount drops 52 to 51, and TC-PATH falls from 13 members to 12. The note was carried across the removal without being updated.

Five operative statements in v5 say the member is unscored and the note contradicts all of them: authored[] no longer contains it; the entry carries no expected key; notAuthored gains a BLOCKED entry for it; whatThisDoesNotDo[6] states 'Does not score TC-PATH unicode-norm-duplicate as proof of the normalization-duplicate arm'; and honestyRepairsFromV4[0] records the unscoring. authorityClaim adds the same sentence.

So the operative state is unambiguous and correct - nothing is actually scored - which is why this is not a blocker. But the false clause sits on the very entry a reader consults to learn this member's standing, in a corpus whose reviewStatus is AWAITING-SATISFIED-GRADE-REVIEW and whose evidentiary value rests on each statement holding.

The artifact shows it knows how to qualify these notes: the notAuthored entry says 'v4 bytes retained under fixtures/dr-103.v4/ as supporting, not scored', and the v4 authored entry it replaced said 'v2/v3 bytes untouched'. This one clause was simply not rebased onto v5.
shouldFix.whyItMatters: At SATISFIED-GRADE the corpus is the acceptance evidence for DR-103's exact-byte cell, and a later reader deciding whether the normalization-duplicate arm is proven will look at this member. An entry asserting it is authored is the one reading the repair exists to prevent.
shouldFix.whyNotABlocker: No member is actually scored by it - there is no expected key, the member is absent from authored, and the count reflects the removal. The defect is a stale clause, not a live scoring claim.
shouldFix.remedy: Replace 'also authored' with the state v5 actually holds, for example 'unscored; retained for directory inventory of v4-only bytes; see notAuthored[TC-PATH unicode-norm-duplicate]'.

repairVerification.finding: CODEX-V4-S1 - the normalization-duplicate fixture remained non-discriminating because its NFD member independently triggers the non-NFC rule
repairVerification.disposition: REPAIRED - VERIFIED, and I confirm Codex's reasoning against the schema
howIChecked: I record first that Codex found this in bytes I accepted at v4. Its reasoning is right and I confirm it: schemas.v11's TC-PATH enumerates 'non-NFC path bytes' and 'Unicode-normalization duplicate path' as separate requirements, RJ-3 carries no subcodes, and the fixture pairs NFC bin/cafe-acute with the NFD form. The NFD member is itself non-NFC, so a validator that checks each path for NFC-ness and never compares paths pairwise after normalization rejects the bytes and passes the fixture. My v3 finding caught the entrypoint mask; this second, subtler mask survived it.

v5's response is to stop scoring rather than to paper over. The member is removed from authored[] entirely - I confirmed by enumerating the array - and authoredCount is reduced from 52 to 51 to match, with TC-PATH falling to 12 members.
The bytes are retained rather than deleted, which is the right call for evidence: the file still exists at fixtures/dr-103.v4/ and is catalogued in supportingBytes with its digest, which recomputes.

The block is recorded with its reason and its exit. notAuthored gains 'TC-PATH unicode-norm-duplicate': 'BLOCKED on schemas.v11 pathRule / RJ-3: a classic NFC/NFD pair is also a non-NFC path. A validator that only rejects non-NFC bytes passes this member without pairwise NFC-uniqueness ... Requires a schema successor (discriminating RJ-3 datum/subcode or an exact normalization relation that permits two individually valid paths to collide) before this member can be scored.' That states the dependency in terms a schema successor can act on, rather than leaving it open-ended.

The claim is repeated where it binds: authorityClaim adds 'TC-PATH unicode-norm-duplicate is not scored as proof of the normalization-duplicate arm', and whatThisDoesNotDo gains the same sentence as a standalone item.

advisories.title: The unscoring dropped v4's predecessorV2 lineage pointer, leaving the superseded v2 copy uncatalogued by this generation
advisories.detail: v4's authored entry carried predecessorV2Path and predecessorV2Sha256 pointing at fixtures/dr-103.v2/TC-PATH.unicode-norm-duplicate.manifest.json at f068504e..., which recorded that the v4 bytes superseded a specific earlier file. v5's replacement supportingBytes entry carries only path, sha256 and note, so that pointer is gone and the v2 copy now appears nowhere in v5's catalog - it is the one file in fixtures/dr-103.v2/ that v5 does not list, 80 of 81 plus the 2 deferred locks. Nothing is wrong with the bytes: I measured the file and it still equals the digest v4 recorded, so it is unmutated, and corpus v3 remains frozen and catalogues it. The loss is of lineage rather than evidence, and it matters mainly because the surviving note claims the entry exists for directory inventory. Restoring the two predecessor keys would keep the supersession traceable from the live generation.
